content.title: About
content.content: Buckwheat is a groat made from the seeds of the common buckwheat plant (Fagopyrum esculentum). Despite its name, it is not a grain and is not related to wheat: it belongs to the knotweed family, like sorrel and rhubarb. Buckwheat has a nutty, slightly earthy flavor. It is cooked as porridge or a side dish, added to soups and salads, and its flour is used for pancakes and noodles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Buckwheat is a pseudocereal: its seeds are used like a grain, but the plant is not a cereal.
Buckwheat is naturally gluten-free, but it may be contaminated with gluten during processing.
Roasted buckwheat is dark and aromatic, while green (unroasted) buckwheat is paler and milder.
Buckwheat flour is used to make pancakes, galettes, and Japanese soba noodles.
Bees make dark, aromatic honey from buckwheat nectar.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Buckwheat contains protein with a good amino acid profile, including lysine, which is low in many grains.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains magnesium, copper, and manganese
items.content: These minerals support muscle and nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains rutin
items.content: Rutin is a flavonoid with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Suitable for gluten-free diets
items.content: Pure buckwheat without cross-contamination can be part of a gluten-free diet when properly labeled.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Buckwheat allergy can be severe and is sometimes linked with latex allergy.

items.title: Gluten contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose buckwheat labeled gluten-free because of possible cross-contamination.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: A sudden increase in fiber intake can cause bloating and discomfort.

items.title: Carbohydrates
items.content: Buckwheat contains carbohydrates, so people with diabetes should keep an eye on portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse buckwheat, add water in a ratio of about 1 to 2, bring to a boil, reduce the heat, and cook covered for 15–20 minutes, then let it stand. Serve it as a side dish or add it to soups, salads, fillings, and patties. Green buckwheat can be soaked and sprouted.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry groats in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Buckwheat flour spoils faster, so keep it in the refrigerator. Store cooked buckwheat in the refrigerator for 3–4 days.
